LANL: first conceived in 1946 by Ulam; during his convalescence, playing solitaire, he asked 'what are the chances that a hand laid out with 52 cards will come out successfully?'; pure combinatorial calculation 'would be monstrously difficult'.
LANL: he could 'simply lay out the cards one hundred times and count the number of successful plays. Implicit was the assumption that each play started with randomized conditions.'
OpenStax 3.1: the long-term relative frequency approaches the theoretical probability 'as the number of repetitions grows larger and larger'.

LANL: developed with von Neumann, first used for neutron diffusion paths; Nick Metropolis coined the name, which referred to Ulam's uncle who would borrow money because he 'just had to go to Monte Carlo'; first calculations ran on ENIAC in April to May 1948.

MWSUG 2010 paper 'Monty Hall, Paul Erdos, and Monte Carlo': Erdos 'did not get the answer right and was only grudgingly convinced of the correct answer after seeing the output from a Monte Carlo simulation'.
Britannica: switching gives a 2/3 chance. Arithmetic checked twice: 3,000 x 2/3 = 2,000.

LANL: its use has exploded into applications in 'science and technology, artificial intelligence, finance, transport, health, and manufacturing, along with virtually every profession that must measure risks'.

Summary of checked claims: odds to probability (UCLA OARC: odds = p/(1-p)); expected value by weighting outcomes (OpenStax 4.2); risk aversion and worst case (Saylor, Avoiding Risk). A checklist framing, not a factual claim beyond these.
Canadian Cancer Society glossary: absolute risk is 'The chance or probability that a person will develop a particular disease over a specific time period.'
OpenStax 3.2: 52 cards in four suits of 13 including hearts, one queen of diamonds. Arithmetic: 13/52 = 25%; 1/52 = 1.9%.
Canadian Cancer Society: absolute risk is the chance of developing a disease 'over a specific time period', so a one-year and a lifetime figure differ.
OpenStax: convert a decimal to a percent by moving the decimal point two places right. Arithmetic: 2/1,000 = 0.002 = 0.2%.
Cancer Research UK: 'Relative risk tells you nothing about actual risk'; the actual risk is the absolute risk.
IWH: 'Relative risk is a comparison between two groups of people ... It can be expressed as a ratio'; a relative risk of one means neither group is more or less likely to be affected.
IWH: relative risk is the ratio of two risks and absolute risk the share affected (e.g. 1 in 1,000 rising to 8 in 1,000). Arithmetic: 2/1 = 2; 2 - 1 = 1 extra per 10,000.
Cancer Research UK: 'for a risk that is quite large already, smaller increases can still have a big impact.' Arithmetic: 1 in 10 = 1,000 per 10,000; 2 in 10 = 2,000; difference 1,000; ratio 2.
Newcastle University (2012): 'Radiation exposure from CT scans in childhood could triple the risk of leukaemia and brain cancer'; a Lancet study 'of more than 175,000 children and young adults'.

Newcastle University: 'for every 10,000 head CT scans performed on children 10 years old or younger, one more case of leukaemia and one more brain tumour would occur than would normally be expected' (Lancet abstract: in the 10 years after the first scan).

Newcastle University: 'The researchers emphasise that when a child suffers a major head injury or develops a life-threatening illness, the benefits of clinically appropriate CT scans should outweigh future cancer risks.'

Cancer Research UK: 'If the initial risk is very small, even a huge increase may not make much absolute difference. But for a risk that is quite large already, smaller increases can still have a big impact.'

WMJ (Calder and Patel): absolute risk of heart attack reduced from 2% (placebo) to 1% is a 50% RRR but an ARD of only 1% in a 2-year study; '100 people like Mrs Smith would have to be treated over a 2-year period to prevent, on average, 1 heart attack.'
WMJ: the number of patients needed to treat (NNT) to prevent some event; 'the calculation always implies a certain follow-up time'.
WMJ: 'This intuitive concept first appeared in medical literature in 1988', citing Laupacis, Sackett and Roberts, N Engl J Med 1988;318:1728-1733.
WMJ: NNT is the reciprocal of the ARD; with risks of 10% and 5% the ARD is 5% and '1 / 0.05 (or 100% / 5%), which equals 20.'
WMJ: NNT = 1/ARD; basketball analogy: 'If my percentage is 25%, I am going to have to go the line 4 times, on average, to make 1 free throw'; 50% needs twice. An ARD of 100% gives NNT 1.
WMJ example: 2% on placebo, 1% on treatment. Arithmetic per 100 treated: 98 would have had no heart attack anyway, 1 has one despite treatment, 1 is spared.

USAFacts (BTS data): 'The 2023 death rate for air passengers was 0.003 deaths per 100 million miles. The rate for car and truck passengers was 0.53.' Of US air travel deaths 2003 to 2023, 72% involved on-demand air taxis and 23% scheduled commercial flights.
problem: The 0.003 figure is USAFacts' rate for all air passengers (including small on-demand air taxis, which account for most air deaths), not for airline passengers specifically. The 'more than 100 times' comparison still holds (0.53/0.003 is about 177, and the airline-only rate is lower still), but labeling 0.003 as the airline rate is imprecise.
proposed: In 2023 US figures, people in cars and trucks died at more than 100 times the rate of air passengers per mile traveled: 0.53 against 0.003 deaths per 100 million passenger miles. (Card 044.c2: change 'the airline passengers' rate' to 'the rate for people traveling by air'.)

evidence: Flight Safety Foundation (Boeing data, 72 fatal accidents 2004 through 2013): 47% in final approach or landing, about 14% in takeoff and initial climb, '10 percent occurred in cruise'.
New Scientist (1999): 'Deaths per 100 million passenger journeys are, on average, 55 for airliners compared with 4.5 for cars'; by distance aircraft look far safer.

New Scientist: compares deaths per distance, 'the number of deaths against the time travelled', and 'the number of deaths with the number of journeys made'; air travel looks safest per distance but riskier per journey.

NIMH: 'Prevalence is the proportion of a population who have a specific characteristic'; it 'may be reported as a percentage (5%, or 5 people out of 100), or as the number of cases per 10,000 or 100,000 people.'
Made-up example using NIMH's prevalence per 10,000. Arithmetic: 1,000 per 10,000 versus 1 per 10,000; if both cause a cough, colds outnumber the rare illness 1,000 to 1 among coughers.
APHL: test results 'should be understood within the context of their environments'; positive predictive value changes 'dramatically depending on the prevalence of the condition within a population.'
